content.comment_body: After a hardwired control box failure on an older machine, I'm considering using a [product_name] unit for a basic control task. My setup involves two inputs: I1 receives a 5V square wave from a rotary encoder (roughly 355 cycles per second) and I2 receives an on-off signal from a sensor (either a photocell or a microswitch, voltage can be chosen). There is one output: O1, which controls a pneumatic solenoid valve operating at either 24V or 240VAC. The logic is: when I2 is active, I want the controller to count a specific number of pulses from I1 before activating O1, then count more pulses before deactivating O1. The programming logic works in the demo software. However, I'm not very experienced with electronics and want to ensure I select the correct model before purchasing. a) Is a 0-5V square wave from the rotary encoder compatible with the [product_name] input? b) Can I use the output of the [product_name] as a normally open switch for the solenoid valve? Also, which [product_name] model should I choose for this application? Looking forward to some advice.

[product_name] 24CE, logic module with display: input/output 24V/24V/24V, 8 digital inputs (4 analog), 4 digital outputs; memory for 400 blocks, expandable, built-in Ethernet web server, data logging on standard micro SD card, compatible with [product_name] programming software. Selecting appropriate hardware depends on your application—for simple on/off tasks like lighting, pumps, fans, or window actuators, choose hardware featuring relay outputs. For functions like dimming or speed control requiring PWM, opt for transistor output hardware. If monitoring values or alarms visually is important, select a model with a display. I suggest the [product_name] [article_no] operating at 12/24V. Standard digital inputs in such controllers typically support up to 4 Hz signals, but models designed for DC supply voltage like the [article_no] feature four high-speed counter inputs processing up to 5 kHz. Note, however, that signal detection requires a high voltage level above 8.5V, so a 5V (TTL) signal won’t be reliably recognized. You might use an optocoupler to adapt the encoder signal. To switch a valve, you could connect a contactor (coil 24VDC) to the controller output; quality contactors can operate with higher voltages like 230V. analysis.insight_summary: Discussions focus on choosing a suitable [product_name] controller to replace a failed wired system for a simple industrial process. Key issues are whether the 5V square wave rotary encoder is directly compatible with the controller inputs and ensuring proper control of pneumatic valves. Responses outline models with relevant input features, clarify potential voltage mismatch on inputs, and suggest solutions like using optocouplers for adaptation. Recommendations detail models and features, but note that direct compatibility with TTL-level signals is a possible limitation needing external circuitry.
analysis.user_expectations: The user expects the [product_name] controller to natively accept a 5V square wave encoder input and provide straightforward switching for solenoid valves. They seek a model recommendation matching simple control logic, easy setup, and minimal electronics expertise.
